LESSON 6 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Security Controls

What a security control is, how controls are classified by function and by type, and why layers — not single products — are what actually stop incidents.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

A security control is any measure that reduces risk. Controls are usually described by when they act: preventive, detective, or responsive. Effective programmes use all three.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Preventive controls stop an attack before it succeeds, such as authentication, authorisation, input validation and network segmentation.
  • Detective controls reveal that something is happening, such as logging, monitoring and file-integrity checking.
  • Responsive controls limit the damage and restore normal service, such as isolation, revocation and tested recovery.
  • Controls are also administrative, technical, or physical, and the classification matters when you assess coverage.
  • Compensating controls reduce risk without removing the underlying weakness, and are legitimate when the real fix is not yet available.

The background

  • Controls existed as physical measures long before computing, and the preventive-detective-responder framing grew out of that tradition.
  • Compliance frameworks in the 1990s turned controls into a checkable list, which made coverage measurable but often reduced controls to paperwork.
  • The concept of defence in depth became central after incidents showed that any single control can fail.
  • Modern frameworks such as the CIS Controls emphasise prioritisation and verification rather than exhaustive control lists.

Real-world examples

  • Multi-factor authentication is preventive, a login alert is detective, and a session revocation process is responsive.
  • A firewall rule that is never tested is documentation, not a control.
  • Backups only count as a control once a restore has been demonstrated, because an untested backup is an assumption.

What to look for

  • For each control, state which risk it addresses and what happens if it fails.
  • Check that detective controls actually alert someone who can act on the alert.
  • Look for controls that exist on paper but are not enforced by tooling.
  • Verify that a control you rely on has been tested recently, not just deployed.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Layer controls so a single failure does not remove a whole protection.
  • Test detective controls by triggering them deliberately in a safe environment.
  • Document the failure mode of every critical control, not just its function.
  • Retire controls that no longer map to a current risk.
